The project includes: • Pedestrian safety enhancements, such as bulb-outs, flashing beacons, and high-visibility striping, at the Grand/ Linda and Grand/Greenbank intersections. • A bicycle turn box with flashing beacon push button at Grand and Linda. • ADA-compliant curb ramps at all street crossings. • Bulb-out islands and a landscaped bioswale at Grand and Fairview — Piedmont’s first “green infrastructure.” These improvements are part of the City’s 2021 Safer Streets Plan, which identified the Grand/ Linda and Grand/Greenbank intersections as two of the top ten priority locations for pedestrian safety improvements citywide. Heavy paving trucks and equipment will make their way to the intersection of Oakland and Grand Avenues starting this Wednesday night.

According to Gidney, the response from the City Council through their negotiator suggested that they were “not interested in discussing retiree medical insurance,” a response that the union found “regrettably offensive and disrespectful.” The second proposal was to provide modest additional compensation, or “longevity pay,” to firefighters who obtained certain service milestones. Common through the fire prevention industry, the practice is meant to provide incentives based upon experience, leading to better performance and ultimately enhanced service to the public. “Our further attempts to negotiate fell on deaf ears and our only option is the contract we have tonight,” said Gidney. “[The contract] makes no progress to ensure a high quality workforce, no progress to ensure the service levels that the residents of Piedmont deserve, no progress to care for the people who care for the city.” “To be clear,” Gidney added, “we are open to solutions, but so far the Council has offered none and disregarded ours.” ROBERT BOSTICK, PHS grad The obvious things are the leaves changing, and it’s cooler. Superintendent High School Courses Throughout the last month, I have written [at Smore.com/n/ gt0zk] about our efforts to align high school course offerings with students interests and needs. To this end, we have reviewed other high-performing high schools to compare course catalogs, we have surveyed students to better understand their course preferences, we have met with high school students to gather informal feedback, and we have discussed at a 9/12 Board Workshop and the 9/22 Board meeting. We have also discussed changes with administrators, teachers, and counselors to broaden our perspective on how the proposed changes may impact students’ high school experience and future college and career opportunities. One point we hear from staff is the concern about student well-being related to the number of AP courses a student may take. That is, if we offer more AP courses, students will feel compelled to take them in order to maximize a student’s effort to take the most rigorous course load available. This is an important point and one we should consider carefully. Will students take all of the APs made available, and will that impact their stress and overall well-being? Given our college-going community, I would acknowledge that the answer is likely yes to both questions. However, the issue [at Go.collegewise.com/school-limits-apclasses#limits] is more complex than whether to offer versus limit APs to ensure student wellness. Local context matters. A key factor to consider is the variety of offerings for students at all grade levels. I would argue that we have done a wonderful job of providing students with a smooth transition from 8th grade to 9th and 10th grade related to rigor. Where we have room for growth is in our non-STEM offerings at all grade levels. This year, we added AP Seminar and opened it up to grade 10 and above. What a wonderful course addition for all grades. Even better, 10th grade students have an AP option in addition to AP Computer Science Principles (another outstanding course, by the way). In order to further open up opportunities for students, at next week’s Board meeting, we will be looking at our high school graduation requirements to eliminate requirements that are not essential to meet the UC A-G requirements. We will also consider additional honors and AP offerings in a variety of subjects. The goal is to expand opportunities for students to explore their interests. One subject that we have few AP options for is History/Social Studies. We currently offer AP US History. Years ago, we offered AP European History; however, after the teacher left, so did the course. A review of similar high schools shows that we are alone in offering only one History/Social Studies AP. Moreover, student survey results indicate a strong desire for AP World History, which we are proposing to the Board as an offering for next fall. Finally, meetings with members of the History/Social Studies department indicate a desire to explore other options for students, including Honors and AP courses. We are excited to continue these conversations. Ultimately, the goal is to enhance student opportunities through course offerings that align with students interests and needs. We are grateful to our staff, students, and parents for their input on our course proposals that we are recommending for approval at Wednesday’s Board meeting. Provide green, open spaces for students and staff to unplug and recharge in a welcoming and natural setting.” To these ends, the identification and development of a plan to cultivate green spaces throughout our campuses is presented in this green space report, prioritized according to two categories: first, locations that are or could be used by students and staff, and second, locations that are perimeter or adjacent spaces that are high traffic and highly visible. articles.text: We all can carry impossibly high standards for ourselves and others. At work, we want to be the leader who always has the right answer. At home, the parent who never loses patience. In community, the friend who shows up flawlessly every time. But here’s the truth: we’re all just humans human-ing — messy, imperfect, trying, failing, learning, and trying again. The sooner we admit that, the freer we become. Imperfection Is a Gift When we drop the myth of perfection, something beautiful happens: people exhale. The meeting that was stiff becomes honest. The team that was afraid to speak up starts sharing bold ideas. The child who thought they had to get it all right suddenly feels safe to experiment. Imperfection doesn’t lower the bar; it creates the trust that makes excellence possible. Giving Ourselves Permission It starts with us. How often do we replay in our heads, over and over again, the awkward moment, the misstep, the thing we should’ve said differently? That loop of self-criticism serves no purpose. So, what if instead we replaced the script with: “I’m just a human human-ing.” We’re all generally trying our best, and that’s all we can ask for. Extending Permission to Others The second step is grace outward. The colleague who missed a deadline. The houseguest who needed more than you expected. The friend who forgot to call. When we remember they’re just human-ing too, it softens our reaction. Compassion doesn’t mean ignoring accountability; it means recognizing that accountability lands best in a culture where mistakes aren’t met with shame, blame, or criticism. Closing Thought Next time you stumble, catch yourself, or catch someone else stumbling, remember: we’re all just humans human-ing. Give yourself and others permission to be imperfect, to learn, to keep going. In the end, we’re never going to reach the bar of “perfect,” so let’s not try. Instead, let’s celebrate the wins, the mistakes, and the in-betweens. articles.text: During the September 24 School Board Meeting Piedmont board trustees, students and teachers met to discuss education in Piedmont, including the State of the School report on Piedmont High School (PHS). Superintendent Jennifer Hawn noted that PHS Principal David Yoshihara sent out the first alumni newsletter, and the negotiations between the district and labor groups, teachers and CSEA unions, began on September 23. On negotiations, this time around, teachers are not negotiating salaries, but are questioning work conditions. The most urgent issue for Piedmont teachers is class size. “Our contract language is unusually weak [in that area],” said APT President Elise Marks about class size. In teacher contracts nothing is specified as to the maximum amount of students in each class, class size maximums are calculated per site, as an average. Nowadays, 5th grade classes average 27 or 28, up from 25 or 26 before the pandemic. Class sizes, when averaged with every class, get under the 28 student on average mark because some classes with unusually small enrollment bring the average under the watermark minimum. Public Comment During the public comment segment of the meeting, PHS senior Elspeth Grippando brought up the absence of a PHS math teacher following a firing. Grippando mentioned that retired teacher Doyle O’Reagan did well in his place but cannot continue. Math Analysis classes have been effected. Grippando explained that a new substitute, Ms. Hook, will take O’Reagan’s place and that Ms. Bailey, PHS art teacher, has been subbing for Math Analysis and plans to until the end of winter break. PHS Math teacher Olesia Parasiuk-Zasun is providing lessons for the substitutes, but not teaching. “These new substitute teachers are disrupting our learning pathways,” said Grippando. “Students need a real math teacher to learn,” she added. Another senior, Malia Williams, addressed the school board to talk about how PHS students don’t have off-campus privileges during the brunch period. Williams proposed offering it as a privilege for students with perfect attendance. Next to the microphone was PHS student, Stella Wilk, whom spoke to the unreliable parking around campus and proposed a student designated parking area. Wilk spoke about the difficulty in student parking directly leading to tardies. Recent changes in parking in the city’s civic center near the pool and police station are factors as well. Mira Sachs, last year’s student representative to the school board, spoke about the usage of Artificial Intelligence, requesting more guidance from the district on policies. “What we don’t have is directed guidance for how AI can be used positively for learning,” said Sachs. Sachs reported to the board there’s no set guidelines, and that students want to work efficiently but don’t know where the line is crossed. Next up for the school board will be a regularly scheduled meeting tonight, October 8, in City Hall at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: When the bell rings at Piedmont High School, students’ phones are supposed to be tucked away. Under the current cell phone policy, phones must remain in backpacks or designated holders during class time, and they’re not to be seen during passing periods or brunch. This change follows Governor Gavin Newsom’s signing of the PhoneFree School Act, which requires every school district, charter school, and county office of education to adopt a policy limiting or prohibiting smartphone use by July 1, 2026. Last year, the rule was simpler: phones had to stay out of sight during class, but students could use them freely during short breaks. Now, students caught with their phones risk having them confiscated for the rest of the day, a shift many, especially juniors and seniors, are still adjusting to. While the policy is meant to improve focus and reduce distractions, its effect on students’ daily lives has been met with an overwhelmingly negative response. “I understand that some people are on their phones too much,” said sophomore Zoya Schulze, “but I feel that texting someone in the hallway shouldn’t get your phone taken away.” Senior Elias Reed-Miguel shared a similar view: “I think we should go back to the policy from last year. There were no problems with it, and if teachers want fewer phones, they could just be stricter about using the cell hotel.” Senior Olive Reining agreed, adding, “I don’t see how the new policy is an improvement from last year. I think kids should be able to use their phones as it’s our time.” The new rules have also changed how students manage stress and downtime. “The phone policy makes us less focused because we’re eager to use our phones more,” said junior Lukas Kim. Most students agree that the cell phone policy is frustrating, but some question whether it actually supports their personal growth. Rather than serving as a teaching tool, many feel it functions more as a punishment, removing the chance for students to learn responsibility and time management on their own. “I think students need to learn how to manage their phone use independently,” said senior Luke McAuliffe. “What works for one person might not work for another.” When asked what they’d like to see moving forward, most students agreed on one thing: they want to be part of the conversation. Despite student board representatives and even some teachers voicing opposition to the new rules last year, those concerns appear to have gone unheard. The policy may aim to reduce screen time and classroom distractions to ease teachers’ workloads, but it could also have the opposite effect. If this rule remains in place throughout high school for current freshmen, it might do more harm than good, limiting students’ ability to self-regulate and prepare for real-world expectations. In a society where technology is deeply woven into everyday life, learning how to use phones responsibly may be more valuable than banning them altogether. Whether the phone policy changes or stays the same, one thing is clear: the current approach feels more like a bandage over a toothache than a real solution. Evolette Mak is a student writer with the Piedmont Post.

Despite student board representatives and even some teachers voicing opposition to the new rules last year, those concerns appear to have gone unheard. The policy may aim to reduce screen time and classroom distractions to ease teachers’ workloads, but it could also have the opposite effect. If this rule remains in place throughout high school for current freshmen, it might do more harm than good, limiting students’ ability to self-regulate and prepare for real-world expectations. Thinking Outside the Classroom Humans Human-ing: Permission to be Imperfect By Nina Meehan We all can carry impossibly high standards for ourselves and others. At work, we want to be the leader who always has the right answer. At home, the parent who never loses patience. In community, the friend who shows up flawlessly every time. But here’s the truth: we’re all just humans human-ing — messy, imperfect, trying, failing, learning, and trying again. The sooner we admit that, the freer we become. Imperfection Is a Gift When we drop the myth of perfection, something beautiful happens: people exhale. The meeting that was stiff becomes honest. The team that was afraid to speak up starts sharing bold ideas. The child who thought they had to get it all right suddenly feels safe to experiment. Imperfection doesn’t lower the bar; it creates the trust that makes excellence possible. Giving Ourselves Permission It starts with us. How often do we replay in our heads, over and over again, the awkward moment, the misstep, the thing we should’ve said differently? That loop of self-criticism serves no purpose. So, what if instead we replaced the script with: “I’m just a human human-ing.” We’re all generally trying our best, and that’s all we can ask for. Extending Permission to Others The second step is grace outward. The colleague who missed a deadline. The houseguest who needed more than you expected. The friend who forgot to call. When we remember they’re just human-ing too, it softens our reaction. Compassion doesn’t mean ignoring accountability; it means recognizing that accountability lands best in a culture where mistakes aren’t met with shame, blame, or criticism. Closing Thought Next time you stumble, catch yourself, or catch someone else stumbling, remember: we’re all just humans human-ing. Give yourself and others permission to be imperfect, to learn, to keep going. In the end, we’re never going to reach the bar of “perfect,” so let’s not try. Instead, let’s celebrate the wins, the mistakes, and the in-betweens. Nina Meehan is a Communication and Creativity Speaker and Coach. https://ninameehan.com/ SPECIAL EVENT! articles.text: PIE presents Understanding Sensory Regulation in Neurodivergent Children Piedmonters for Inclusive Education (PIE) kick off their annual Neurodiversity Speaker Series with a session on Understanding Sensory Regulation in Neurodivergent Children. The virtual event will be held on Tuesday, October 28 from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m. RSVP at Uclawsf.zoom. us/meeting/register/4aJnivLMSDOux50lIeMF0Q#/registration to receive the Zoom link. About the event: When children show big behaviors such as throwing things, leaving the group, or struggling to sit at dinner, it’s often a sign of being overwhelmed, not defiance. This talk will reframe behavior as communication and explore how sensory differences can impact regulation at home and in school. Parents will learn how to become “sensory detectives,” spotting cues of overwhelm, building trust through connection, and using practical tools, from sensory breaks to emotional regulation strategies to support children to thrive. The event will discuss ways to set loving limits, foster resilience, and create environments where kids can meet their full potential. About the speaker: Lee-Anne Bloom, MS, OTR/L is the founder of Oak Bloom OT in Oakland. She helps children thrive through a strengths-based approach that blends play, creativity, interest exploration, and mindful awareness. With expertise in ADHD, Autism, and Sensory Processing differences, she supports kids in building skills, resilience, and confidence while adapting environments for sensory and emotional needs. As both a professional and a parent of a neurodivergent child, she is passionate about de-stigmatizing neurodiversity. About PIE: Founded in 1999, PIE is a volunteer-run community of parents committed to advancing equity and inclusion for children with disabilities and learning differences in Piedmont schools. PIE works alongside families, educators, and the school district to strengthen the schools, foster understanding and acceptance, and provide a supportive network for families. Visit www.piedmontie.org to learn more.

articles.text: This fall, six seniors from Piedmont High School were recognized as National Merit Semifinalists, an honor awarded to the top one percent of high school juniors nationwide based on their PSAT/NMSQT scores. “I felt pretty good coming out of the test, so I was just happy when I saw I got semifinalist,” said Nathan Tuan. “I prepared by doing Khan Academy and the Blue Book tests, and some College Board problems that you can find on their website.” Another semifinalist, Athena Li, reflected on her preparation with a casual approach. “I did the two practice PSATs on College Board a little while beforehand. I honestly wasn’t aiming for it, I just thought I’d take the test and see how I’d do.” The National Merit Scholarship Program recognizes academic excellence and gives students the opportunity to advance to the finalist stage, where they can compete for scholarships totaling more than $30 million nationwide. However, beyond the prestige, the financial reward is not as significant as many might assume. “Being a semifinalist does not affect my college plans at all. They don’t really give that much money,” said Maddox Ma. “It’s like $2,500 one time, so not enough to make an impact.” Given the sheer difficulty and rarity of becoming a semifinalist, many find it surprising that such an achievement yields a relatively modest monetary reward, especially considering the soaring cost of college tuitions today. The $2,500 scholarship, while symbolic of academic excellence, barely makes a dent in the financial reality of higher education, where a single semester’s tuition can easily exceed twenty times that amount. Still, the recognition carries value beyond numbers. Earning a spot among the top one percent of test takers nationwide is less a financial victory than a reflection of persistence, preparation, and curiosity. In an academic world often driven by outcomes, the National Merit distinction reminds students that the pursuit of knowledge still holds meaning on its own. articles.text: The Piedmont High School Class of 1960 held its 65th reunion on September 20 at the Moraga Country Club. There were 49 attendees, 35 of whom were from the class, and five who still make their home in Piedmont. The event began at noon with a number of people arriving early. The camaraderie started immediately with a warm greeting of “it’s so good to see you,” followed by hugs. The event was to be from noon to four and included a lovely buffet of salmon, chicken, and delicious salads. There was no planned program except a short introduction by Matt Lifschiz, the “Chairman of the Reunion Committee”. The latter is a group of 18 classmates who have enjoyed getting together for many years to plan the event. This class is a little unusual as they don’t seem to wait every 5 years, as is customary. In fact, they had a reunion last year at the same venue, and everyone had such a good time that they said to do it again in 2025. Since their 50th reunion in 2010, this group has had at least six “reunions”. A couple were in a private home, and the others were at various restaurants, including Trader Vic’s. The latter was also the site of a special birthday tribute to one of their favorite teachers, Jim Killian, and included members from the classes of ‘59 and ‘61. Besides residents of Southern and Northern California, guests came from Oregon, Idaho, Nevada and Pennsylvania. As the afternoon started to wind down, the quiet buzz around the room was that this was probably going to be the last reunion, as the committee is getting tired. The buzz got louder, and the wishes were heard that the majority would love another get-together, even if it could be something simple in a private home. This Class of ‘60 loves being together and sharing what’s happening, where they are living, and what they are doing. So, who knows? It might happen again next year or if not, surely in two years. PHS 1960 classmates still living in Piedmont include Gage Lund Herman (left), Liz Land Silverman, Stan Silverman, Fran Bishopric Wolfe, and Matt Lifschiz.
articles.title: PHS Class of ’60 celebrates 65th reunion

Piedmont Cross Country Teams Strong in Early Meets Piedmont High’s cross country teams competed in two events over the past week, including their first Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season at Point Pinole Regional Park on Wednesday, Oct. 1, and the Artichoke Invitational at Half Moon Bay High School on Saturday, Oct. 4. The Highlander boys won the WACC meet in a field of nine schools, while the girls finished fourth of nine. At the Artichoke Invitational, Piedmont’s girls placed fourth of 19 teams in the small schools division, and the boys were seventh of 27. “The varsity girls’ team had a very good team performance again on Saturday,” coach Steve Zirkelbach said. Filling in for Zirkelbach at the league meet was assistant coach Leighton Mand charges her way up a hill at the Artichoke Invitational. and PHS alum Sophia Mills. “This one is always a fun one with some added challenges like the massive hill and a few hay bales to hurdle,” Mills said. “A highlight for me once again was the tight spread of the varsity boys squad, about 30 seconds from first to fifth runner.” The Highlanders now look ahead to the Asics Clovis Invitational at Woodward Park, which is also the site of the CIF State Championships, on Oct. 10-11. The long-running event, now in its 46th year, will bring together hundreds of athletes from across California. Artichoke Invitational Junior Leighton Mand led the girls with a 16th-place finish among 158 runners, clocking 15:11 on the 2.3-mile course. Senior Skylar Best followed in 20th at 15:26, and junior Amalia Gray was close behind in 22nd at 15:35. Sophomore Nikita Gorelik placed 33rd (15:58), and sophomore Viviane Oesterer rounded out Piedmont’s top five in 55th (16:34). articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team reeled in two wins over the past week to improve their record to 8-8 overall. They recently defeated Western Alameda County Conference foe, Berkeley, in a clean 7-0 sweep at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Thursday, October 2, while they beat Marin Catholic 5-2 on Tuesday, September 30. The Highlanders’ win over Berkeley improved their league record to 2-1 with five WACC matches left in the regular season before the league’s individual tournament on November 7-8. Ruthven has been Piedmont’s top singles starter for the season, a rarity for a freshman newcomer. “It’s really fun playing singles. The team has been really fun and super supportive. As the No. 1 singles starter, Ruthven has had her share of difficult matches, including g a narrow loss to Marin Catholic, 7-6 (10-8), 6-4. Despite taking on some of the best competition throughout the North Coast Section, Ruthven is keeping a positive perspective. “It’s definitely pushing me harder because a lot of my competition is older and bigger than me, but it just pushes to use my strengths and work on the things I need to work on. articles.text: It was a defensive battle for Piedmont, falling in a narrow 13-0 battle to Berkeley. Piedmont High’s flag football team traveled to Berkeley High on Monday, Oct. 6, falling 13-0 in a tough defensive matchup. The loss brings the Highlanders’ record to 4-8 overall, with four games remaining in the season. “Their coach came over and said our defense figured us out. We held them scoreless through three quarters, so that was impressive,” coach Beth Black said. “We made a lot of adjustments from our last game, and the players are applying them. It’s a bummer it’s not turning into wins.” The game marked quarterback Edie Elmquist’s return to the position after an injury forced her out for the previous two games. It was also Piedmont’s third straight contest without scoring points. “Edie had a sore arm, so she Staff Photos Kate Tong had an interception in the third quarter. didn’t throw before, but she threw well tonight and was connecting on more passes,” Black said. It was also a strong night for receiver Stephanie Lee, who caught eight passes. “Stephanie was making plays. She made good turns on the flat and really dipped her hips to avoid flag pulls. She’s good on both sides of the ball,” Black said. Stephanie Lee led the team with eight receptions.

articles.text: Piedmont girls split league matches Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team split a pair of Western Alameda County Conference road matches last week, beating Encinal 3–1 on Sept. 30 before falling 3–0 to Castro Valley on Oct. 2. Maiki Ting and Stella Wilk powered the Highlanders past Encinal, combining for 30 kills: 17 from Ting and 13 from Wilk. Against league champion Castro Valley, sophomore Olivia Stevens led the team with 12 kills. She also anchored the defense versus Encinal with 25 digs. The Highlanders now stand at 8–6 overall and 1–3 in league play. With five matches left in the regular season, they need two more wins to automatically clinch a North Coast Section playoff berth, their first since 2018. 3–1 over Encinal All four sets were tight, each decided by five points or fewer. After dropping the opener 25–23, Piedmont won the next three, 25–20, 25–22, 25–23. Wilk opened strong with five kills and a block in the first set. Ting and Wilk each had four kills in the second, and Mira Sachs added two kills and a block. Ting led the way down the stretch with six kills in the third set and seven more in the fourth. articles.text: Mark Kliszewski is known in Piedmont by two very different titles: Judge and Coach. By profession, he has spent four decades in the law, serving since 1985 as a Juvenile Court Referee for the Alameda Superior Court. His guiding principle is simple but powerful: young people deserve guidance, not just punishment. a volunteer who has devoted thousands of hours to coaching youth sports, including football, basketball, baseball, softball, and soccer. His players know him not only as a coach but as a mentor who builds discipline, confidence, and teamwork. Born in Overton, Wales, in 1949 to Polish parents who were liberated from Nazi concentration camps, Coach K came to the United States as a child. In Los Angeles, his parents became leaders in the Polish community, especially in Scouting and education, leaving a lasting impression of service that shaped his life. His impact has been widely recognized. In 1986, the City of Piedmont named him Outstanding Volunteer for his service to youth, and in 1991, he received the Service to Youth Award from the Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America and the Sidney C. Singer family. These honors reflect not only his dedication to the law and the playing field, but also his lifelong devotion to helping young people succeed. Q: How did you first get involved with Piedmont High School football, and what was the program like when you started? Coach K: My son entered Piedmont Middle School as a pretty good football player. The head of the Rec Dept saw that, and, since a coach was needed for their teams, asked me to take on the 7th and then 8th grade teams. I did that for three years. Then Mark Kliszewski, known as “Coach K”, pictured in 2008. every season, and freshman players who had never played before entering high school. And we beat the cream of the crop around the Bay Area. It was truly wonderful and eventually led to some terrific varsity teams. Q: How has the role of student-athletes changed at Piedmont, especially when it comes to balancing academics and athletics? Coach K: I don’t believe that the student athlete has changed much. Piedmont students have always done very well academically, with many on the honor roll and having great success in school and in life. There are always some knuckleheads, but no one has been extraordinarily Coach K in 1969. Coach [Mike] Humphries, who was a good friend, asked that I join him in coaching the Freshman team at Piedmont High. I’ve stayed with one of the high school teams pretty much ever since. Q: What major changes have you seen in the football program over the decades—in terms of culture, coaching style, or player development? Coach K: When I began, football was a big deal in Piedmont. We played in a very tough league, and always did well. We had 3 teams of up to 40 players on each. Varsity and JV practiced on the big field and frosh were on the baseball outfield. It was great for development, as kids would come in with virtually no knowledge or ability, and would be ready for varsity before junior year. The culture was great. Witter was pretty much packed every Friday home night, and a band and cheerleaders were always there. On Homecoming there’d be a parade around the field, a contest between classes for best float, announcement of homecoming king and queen, a huge rally in the gym, etc. Generally, Piedmont was the same over summers, with coaches trying to get players to come to practices, and Piedmont families travelling all over the place. Coaching went from very good to pretty bad, as coaches were paid very little, and some just weren’t into it after a while. Our frosh program was great, because Mike Humphries stayed 48 years and I tagged along for 24. Q: How has the community’s involvement or support for the football program changed over the years? Coach K: Football has always been popular in Piedmont. There are fans, and they like to come out Friday nights and enjoy games. Teams were up and down most years, but community support has been pretty solid. Unfortunately, it has become difficult to get players to join the program. In the seventies and eighties, football was king. Since about 2010 there has been a slide. That can be attributed to several factors. Water polo and cross country have taken kids out of football to join their high school teams. Other season sports like basketball, lacrosse, swimming, baseball, etc. have attracted potential players to outside club teams who have insisted that they come to daily practices after school, thus eliminating them from football. Additionally, kids themselves, and oftentimes parents, have become very concerned about football injuries, and have opted not to play. And, of course, when COVID came along, football was very affected by the “no nearness” rules and barely hung on for three or four years. This is all exacerbated by the fact that there just aren’t enough students at PHS to fill all the teams. Luckily, the program has made a big comeback in the last 2 years and there is good hope for a future rebound. Q: Are there any particular seasons or games that stand out to you as especially meaningful or memorable? Why? Coach K: When I coached the frosh with Mike Humphries, we had an incredible run. We actually won 36 straight games over 5 years. This with a new class bad, and many have been very successful. Q: What are some of the biggest challenges the program has faced, and how did the team overcome them? Coach K: The COVID crisis of 2019-21 was very difficult. We were unable to play football. We could line up and run plays with our masks on, but we couldn’t get close to each other, or even use a ball. Practices were pretty ridiculous and players began to stop coming. We only had about 15-18 players on varsity so games were almost impossible to play. JV had about the same numbers. After 5 games varsity had to give up its season. Luckily, many of the varsity players were sophomores, so they were placed on JV and we managed to complete the JV season. That kept kids playing and did a lot to save football in Piedmont. Q: What values or lessons do you hope players take away from being part of the Piedmont football program? Coach K: Football is a pretty unique sport. All 11 players on the field have to be in sync for there to be success. If one player does the wrong thing, a play falls apart. This is a great lesson for life. Coordinating with other people, helping when someone needs help, working together towards a common goal, befriending others whom you may not know, all qualities that are begun in, and carried forward, from football. Also, hard work is learned and hopefully continued after football ends. Q: Have there been any traditions, rituals, or team habits that have stuck with the program across generations? Coach K: Each team has its own personality. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, October 8, 2025 By Jason Shum Mark Kliszewski is known in Piedmont by two very different titles: Judge and Coach. By profession, he has spent four decades in the law, serving since 1985 as a Juvenile Court Referee for the Alameda Superior Court. His guiding principle is simple but powerful: young people deserve guidance, not just punishment. By passion, he is “Coach K,” a volunteer who has devoted thousands of hours to coaching youth sports, including football, basketball, baseball, softball, and soccer. His players know him not only as a coach but as a mentor who builds discipline, confidence, and teamwork. Born in Overton, Wales, in 1949 to Polish parents who were liberated from Nazi concentration camps, Coach K came to the United States as a child. In Los Angeles, his parents became leaders in the Polish community, especially in Scouting and education, leaving a lasting impression of service that shaped his life. His impact has been widely recognized. In 1986, the City of Piedmont named him Outstanding Volunteer for his service to youth, and in 1991, he received the Service to Youth Award from the Piedmont Council of the Boy Scouts of America and the Sidney C. Singer family. These honors reflect not only his dedication to the law and the playing field, but also his lifelong devotion to helping young people succeed. Q: How did you first get involved with Piedmont High School football, and what was the program like when you started? Coach K: My son entered Piedmont Middle School as a pretty good football player. The head of the Rec Dept saw that, and, since a coach was needed for their teams, asked me to take on the 7th and then 8th grade teams. I did that for three years. Then Mark Kliszewski, known as “Coach K”, pictured in 2008. every season, and freshman players who had never played before entering high school. And we beat the cream of the crop around the Bay Area. It was truly wonderful and eventually led to some terrific varsity teams. Q: How has the role of student-athletes changed at Piedmont, especially when it comes to balancing academics and athletics? Coach K: I don’t believe that the student athlete has changed much. Piedmont students have always done very well academically, with many on the honor roll and having great success in school and in life. There are always some knuckleheads, but no one has been extraordinarily Coach K in 1969. An Interview with Mark Kliszewski (Coach K) Coach [Mike] Humphries, who was a good friend, asked that I join him in coaching the Freshman team at Piedmont High. I’ve stayed with one of the high school teams pretty much ever since. Q: What major changes have you seen in the football program over the decades—in terms of culture, coaching style, or player development? Coach K: When I began, football was a big deal in Piedmont. We played in a very tough league, and always did well. We had 3 teams of up to 40 players on each. Varsity and JV practiced on the big field and frosh were on the baseball outfield. It was great for development, as kids would come in with virtually no knowledge or ability, and would be ready for varsity before junior year. The culture was great. Witter was pretty much packed every Friday home night, and a band and cheerleaders were always there. On Homecoming there’d be a parade around the field, a contest between classes for best float, announcement of homecoming king and queen, a huge rally in the gym, etc. Generally, Piedmont was the same over summers, with coaches trying to get players to come to practices, and Piedmont families travelling all over the place. Coaching went from very good to pretty bad, as coaches were paid very little, and some just weren’t into it after a while. Our frosh program was great, because Mike Humphries stayed 48 years and I tagged along for 24. Q: How has the community’s involvement or support for the football program changed over the years? Coach K: Football has always been popular in Piedmont. There are fans, and they like to come out Friday nights and enjoy games. Teams were up and down most years, but community support has been pretty solid. Unfortunately, it has become difficult to get players to join the program. In the seventies and eighties, football was king. Since about 2010 there has been a slide. That can be attributed to several factors. Water polo and cross country have taken kids out of football to join their high school teams. Other season sports like basketball, lacrosse, swimming, baseball, etc. have attracted potential players to outside club teams who have insisted that they come to daily practices after school, thus eliminating them from football. Additionally, kids themselves, and oftentimes parents, have become very concerned about football injuries, and have opted not to play. And, of course, when COVID came along, football was very affected by the “no nearness” rules and barely hung on for three or four years. This is all exacerbated by the fact that there just aren’t enough students at PHS to fill all the teams. Luckily, the program has made a big comeback in the last 2 years and there is good hope for a future rebound. Q: Are there any particular seasons or games that stand out to you as especially meaningful or memorable? Why? Coach K: When I coached the frosh with Mike Humphries, we had an incredible run. We actually won 36 straight games over 5 years. This with a new class bad, and many have been very successful. Q: What are some of the biggest challenges the program has faced, and how did the team overcome them? Coach K: The COVID crisis of 2019-21 was very difficult. We were unable to play football. We could line up and run plays with our masks on, but we couldn’t get close to each other, or even use a ball. Practices were pretty ridiculous and players began to stop coming. We only had about 15-18 players on varsity so games were almost impossible to play. JV had about the same numbers. After 5 games varsity had to give up its season. Luckily, many of the varsity players were sophomores, so they were placed on JV and we managed to complete the JV season. That kept kids playing and did a lot to save football in Piedmont. All 11 players on the field have to be in sync for there to be success. If one player does the wrong thing, a play falls apart. This is a great lesson for life. Coach K: Each team has its own personality. Players between 14 and 18 years old have quirks and differences, but it’s pretty clear that almost everyone wants to better himself, get stronger, and win games. That never changes. Q: If you could leave future players with one piece of advice or one story that represents what Piedmont football is about, what would it be? Coach K: No matter how much you try, or even fail, stick with it. You can always make yourself better. You can always learn more. You can always challenge yourself to achieve the next goal. articles.text: Branford Marsalis Quartet The Branford Marsalis Quartet, one of the longest-running and most acclaimed ensembles in modern jazz, performs four concerts at Miner Auditorium in San Francisco October 23 through 26. The quartet returns to San Francisco to perform a range of music including a selection of the Keith Jarrett compositions that make up his 2025 Blue Note debut Belonging. Led by saxophonist Branford Marsalis, a Grammy-winning saxophonist and national Jazz Master, the quartet currently includes pianist Joey Calderazzo, bassist Eric Revis and drummer Justin Faulkner. Calderazzo and Revis joined the group in the 1990s, while Faulkner became the newest member in 2009. Marsalis, the group’s founder, is a highly regarded composer and jazz tenor saxophonist who comes from a lineage of jazz greats hailing from New Orleans. He is the eldest son of pianist and educator Ellis Marsalis, and his brothers Wynton, Jason and Delfeayo are all well-known musicians in the genre. Marsalis’ vast repertoire includes works by Copland, Debussy, Glazunov, Ibert, Mahler, Milhaud, Rorem, Vaughn Williams, Villa-Lobos and Sally Beamish. He is often a guest with leading symphony orchestras including those in Chicago, Detroit, Dusseldorf and North Carolina as well as the New York Philharmonic. Formed in 1986, the Branford Marsalis Quartet has remained a central outlet for Marsalis’ artistic vision, blending post-bop traditions with innovative improvisation and modern sensibilities. The group’s discography includes Braggtown (2006), Four MFs Playin’ Tunes (2012), and The Secret Between the Shadow and the Soul (2019). The Branford Marsalis Quartet performs at Miner Auditorium, presented by SFJAZZ, Thursday, October 23 through Sunday, October 26. All concerts begin at 7:30 p.m. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/.

articles.text: Mezzo-soprano Daniela Mack joins the San Francisco Opera to perform a program of Manuel de Falla songs and Ludwig van Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony on Saturday, November 1, at the War Memorial Opera House. This one-night only concert begins with Manuel de Falla’s music from Siete Canciones Populares Españolas, inspired by his home country of Spain, and an arrangement of the second orchestral suite from his ballet El Sombrero de Tres Picos (The Three-Cornered Hat) (1917). The orchestra will perform Beethoven’s iconic Fifth Symphony after intermission. “The San Francisco Opera Orchestra and I customarily work together in the orchestra pit, but these musicians, due to their vast experience, can also command the stage. In our fall concert, the Orchestra will do just that in Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony,” Music Director Eun Sun Kim said in a press release. Kim added that Manuel de Falla “absorbed Beethoven’s influence, even citing the famous ‘fate’ motif from the Fifth SymDaniela Mack phony in his ballet.” Falla’s song cycle will feature mezzo-soprano Mack, a native of Buenos Aires who has gained critical acclaim as a classic soloist. She starred as Frida Kahlo in San Francisco Opera’s first Spanish-language opera, Gabriela Lena Frank and Nilo Cruz’s El último sueño de Frida y Diego (The Last Dream of Frida and Diego), in June 2023. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. For tickets and more information, contact the San Francisco Opera Box Office at 301 Van Ness Avenue, call (415) 864-3330 or visit at sfopera.com.

articles.text: Musical runs from Nov. 15 - Dec. 30 at Ashby Stage Shotgun Players closes out its 2025 season with a new production of Sunday in the Park with George, the Pulitzer Prize–winning musical by Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine, showing November 15 through December 30 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. Directed by Susannah Martin with music direction by David Möschler, the show is inspired by Georges Seurat’s pointillist painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte. The musical explores the artist’s obsessive creative process and its impact on his relationships. The production features immersive on-stage seating and an expanded bar menu. “This musical captures the questioning, fear, joy, and obsession that go into making art and the toll it takes on the people we love,” Director Susannah Martin said in a press release. “I’ve never experienced a musical which gets so deeply into the experience of being an artist and the process of making art.” “The sound-world of the show is just as daring, provocative, interesting, and non-traditional as the type of art that the character of George Seurat was striving to create,” added Möschler. “It’s not book scenes followed by songs belted out ad nauseum; it’s a score that is interwoven through dialogue and comes together more like a film score that helps create a strong sense of narrative and dramatic continuity from beginning to end.” Kevin Singer stars as George, with Marah Sotelo as Dot. The cast includes Alex Rodriguez, Laura Domingo, Jill Slyter and a 16-member ensemble. Artistic Director Patrick Dooley called the work a “legitimate masterpiece,” adding, “Sondheim captures the tension between artist and muse, beautifully and tragically.” Tickets and performance details are available at shotgunplayers.org.
articles.title: Shotgun Players closes season with Sondheim’s Sunday in the Park with George

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco’s newest exhibition, UNBOUND: Art, Blackness, and the Universe, is now on view. UNBOUND is a unique group exhibition that explores connections between Blackness and spiritual cosmologies. Organized by Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, the community retrospective highlights the similarities between the Black existence and “cosmic Blackness,” or Afrofuturism. UNBOUND includes paintings, glass sculptures, and installations celebrating the modern artistic genre. The exhibition features artists David Alabo, Renee Cox, Oasa DuVerney, Torkwase Dyson, Allison Janae Hamilton, Barkley L. Hendricks, Cullen B. Washington Jr., M. Carmen Lane and Sidra Bell, Michi Meko, Gustavo Nazareno, Rashaad Newsome, Chris Ofili, Mikael Owunna, Harmonia Rosales, Lorna Simpson, Didier William, and Fred Wilson. “For the past twenty years, MoAD has proudly embarked on a journey to ensure that Black creative expression is embraced, elevated, and seen by international visitors and those that call the Bay Area home,” said Monetta White, Executive Director and CEO. “The artistic depth of UNBOUND will bring intergenerational African Diasporic voices together under an innovative curatorial framework that shifts the focus through which we understand and appreciate contemporary art.” “This exhibition is a celebration of the vast conceptual capacity of Blackness, and treats Black existence with the same imaginative and intellectual openness we apply to thinking through metaphysics and the cosmos,” Lee added. “In doing so, it makes a radical claim that Blackness is not marginal, but central to how we comprehend being, time, and the universe itself.” For more information, visit https://www.moadsf.org. Allison Janae Hamilton is one of over a dozen Black artists featured in MoAD’s UNBOUND.
articles.title: UNBOUND: Art, Blackness and the Universe now on view at MoAD

articles.text: Last Weekend! to Oct. 13, 11–2 p.m. Slavic Arts Exhibition The Center for Slavic Arts and Culture is proud to present its very first exhibition, KALEIDOSCOPE. The show brings together 17 artists from five Slavic countries, including a photographer and a jewelry designer, each sharing their talent and creative vision. In challenging and uncertain times, art reminds us of beauty, resilience, and the strength of our community. Kaleidoscope is a celebration of creativity, and a reminder of how art can connect, uplift, and inspire us all. This exhibition will be open weekend days from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. until mid-October. articles.text: “Suspension of disbelief” is a term often invoked when discussing certain genres of literature, film, or art. Coined by poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge in 1817, it originally referred to “poetic faith”—the idea that audiences willingly set aside skepticism to engage with a story’s imaginative world. Over time, the phrase has evolved to encompass a wide range of creative expressions. As defined today, it is the audience’s conscious decision to overlook logical inconsistencies and accept the impossible—whether in fantasy, fiction, or science fiction— so they can become emotionally immersed in an artist’s reality-bending vision. In short, it’s the act of believing there is something beyond the evidence. E.M. Forster captured this idea beautifully when he wrote: “For human intercourse, as soon as we look at it for its own sake and not as a social adjunct, is seen to be haunted by a specter… what we call intimacy is only a makeshift, perfect knowledge is an illusion. But in the novel we can know people perfectly… Fiction is truer than history for it goes beyond the evidence.” Children, of course, are natural masters of this art. Because their understanding of logic and physics is still forming, the line between reality and imagination remains soft. Their ability to believe, to accept the fantastic without hesitation, is what allows them to connect so deeply with stories of wonder. This is the foundation on which studios like Pixar, Ghibli, Disney, DreamWorks, and Warner Bros. have built their magic. Their films rely on anthropomorphism, imbuing animals or objects with human qualities, and on the limitless possibilities of animation and CGI. From the Marvel Universe to post-apocalyptic fiction, from The Time Traveler’s Wife to The Age of Adaline, audiences routinely embrace the impossible: superheroes, ghosts, aliens, spirits, and worlds that bend the laws of time and nature. For adults, grounded in science and logic, it can be tempting to dismiss such imaginative leaps. But encouraging children to suspend disbelief—to believe in Santa Claus and his flying reindeer, in elves at the North Pole, in worlds unseen—nurtures more than just creativity. Some psychologists suggest that imagination itself is linked to empathy: the capacity to share and understand the feelings of others. In that sense, the willingness to believe in something beyond the evidence may not only enrich art—it may also deepen our humanity. Their robberies attract the attention of two Texas Rangers— Marcus Hamilton (Jeff Bridges), a grizzled veteran on the brink of retirement, and his partner Alberto Parker (Gil Birmingham). As they track the brothers from dusty town to dusty town, they trade dry banter and weary insights about the changing world around them. If you’re a fan of the Coen brothers’ No Country for Old Men, you’ll find much to admire here. The brothers’ love and resentment play out with a mix of grit and tenderness, while the Rangers’ easy-going ribbing masks affection forged through years on the road. Beyond its sharp dialogue and tense pacing, Hell or High Water offers a pointed look at rural America’s economic despair. Behind the faded façades of these small towns lies a quiet anger— ordinary people trying to keep their heads above water as the system fails them. The final act delivers both a satisfying twist and a somber inevitability. Every performance shines—Bridges once again proves his mastery, Pine brings quiet depth, and Foster delivers a live-wire unpredictability that keeps the film pulsing to the end. Hell or High Water. With its lush watercolor palette and Hawaiian setting, it’s a story that’s both whimsical and deeply human—family-friendly, poignant, and occasionally beguiling. articles.text: The Historic Pardee Home Museum and the National Women’s History Alliance (NWHA) are inviting community members to join them in recognizing the 114th Anniversary of the triumph of California suffragists winning passage of the pivotal Suffrage Amendment to the State Constitution in the 1919 election. This community event will be held at Oakland’s Pardee Home Museum in downtown Oakland, 672 11th Street, on October 4th at 1:00 p.m. The program will feature presentations, refreshments and a rousing California Women’s Suffrage Campaign Readers’ Theatre. Several local volunteers, representing individual suffragists, female and male, will briefly present the dramatic story of the challenges and campaigns women endured from their defeat in 1896 to their victory on October 10, 1911. As part of the celebration there will be a Tour of the Pardee Home Museum, one of California’s architectural and historical treasures. The beauty of the home museum and its gardens is striking. The stunning interior of the house showcases artifacts from throughout the world. Featured in the collection is a classic particularly relevant to this celebration: a unique First Edition of “The History of the Woman Suffrage” distinguished by a special lengthy inscription by Susan B. Anthony herself lobbying Governor Pardee to support California women’s right to vote. It’s only one thing to savor and enjoy at this special event. Admission to this California Suffrage Celebration is $25 and supports the Pardee Home Museum and the NWHA’s work. articles.text: World adventurer and coach of disabled and able-bodied athletes, Terry Cotter passed away on September 14, 2025. He was 84. Ralph Evans Cotter III, always known as Terry, passed away peacefully on Sunday, September 14 at Stanford Hospital. Terry was born on September 12, 1941 as the son of Mr. and Mrs. Ralph E. Cotter, Jr., of Oakland, and grandson of Major and Mrs. Winfield S. Overton of Piedmont and Mr. and Mrs. Ralph E. Cotter, Sr., of Oakland. Terry attended Montclair Elementary School, then Piedmont Jr. and Sr. High School. He then studied at Menlo College and graduated from Arizona State University with a major in journalism. He also served in the California National Guard. His life-long passion for Africa and animal conservation developed in high school when he first traveled to Africa with his aunt, uncle and cousins. After college, he went back on a solo motorcycle journey riding from Germany to the southernmost part of Africa. This adventure turned his interest from journalism to travel and he opened the International Travel Guild in San Francisco where he specialized in African tours and treks. Later in his life, his great love for African animals led him to meaningful work with Safari West in Sonoma County, California, and White Oak, the internationally recognized conservation center in Yulee, Florida. Terry dedicated his life to coaching disabled and able-bodied athletes across the globe. An avid cyclist, he helped lead charitable rides such as Best Buddies, Sea to Shining Sea, and Face Across America, each dedicated to improving the lives of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. He served as a Team Leader for The Vietnam Challenge, a transformative bicycle journey that brought together able-bodied and disabled American and Vietnamese veterans riding from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City. His leadership also extended to AXA Worldride 1995, a 13,000- mile global bicycle journey with 10,000 participants-disabled and able-bodied-riding together across continents. It was during Worldride that he met his beloved wife, Eliza Cotter, who matched his energy and enthusiasm for so many wonderful adventures. He guided and encouraged athletes on some of the most inspiring stages, including carrying the Olympic Torch for the 1984 Los Angeles Games and the Paralympic Torch at the 1996 Atlanta Paralympics, where he also coached the Afghan Paralympic Bicycling Team. He coached Special Olympics track and field in Marin County for over 30 years and taught adaptive skiing at Achieve Tahoe in Lake Tahoe for six seasons. He climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro five times, twice leading Special Olympic athletes on the trek. He is survived by his wife Eliza Cotter, his sister Susan Johnson, and his daughter Hannah Cotter. He is also survived by his step-children, grandchildren, and many nieces, nephews and their children, all of whom he loved dearly. To honor Terry’s legacy, the family kindly requests that donations be made to the Safari West Wildlife Fountain at safariwestwildlifefoundation.org.

articles.text: In the last few years, the Piedmont Center for the Arts Artisanal Beer Festival organizers noticed that more guests were enjoying the late Fall vibe on PCA’s front lawn. In fact, more than a few patrons brought blankets. So last year PCA decided to include a trio of Piedmont High students playing some cool jazz. And as the evening wore on, the front lawn scene drew more patrons and started to look like an outdoor music festival. Organizers even learned that some patrons just came to enjoy the music. Jazz lovers are in for another treat this year. After rave reviews from last year’s crowd, the PCA is pleased to announce that last year’s jazz combo will return this year – Deniz Radzik, Eric Verner and Maxim Miller. While they are all PHS students, each has been playing music for some time. Deniz Radzik’s father was a musician, and Deniz started playing violin in 4th grade. However, he ended up playing percussion and drums in the middle school concert and jazz band. As he entered high school, he played with several California jazz conservatory bands. Eric Venner also comes from a musical family. His mother sang in the choir at Boston University where she met Eric’s father, who sang in the Stanford A Capella group. Eric started playing classical guitar at age eight and switched to blues, jazz, and funk guitar at age 12, He is now part of the PHS jazz combo. Maximo Miller started playing piano at age seven with the encouragement of his parents and switched to jazz when he was 12. He plays in the PHS jazz band, and gigs around the area with the sophomore combo. This year’s Beer Festival takes place on Friday, October 23 from 5:30-7:30 p.m. The beer tasting takes place inside the center. Admission is $15 and includes a custom PCA beer glass. The traditional Oktoberfest meal, donated by Piedmont Grocery, is also $15 and is served of the PCA lawn. Credit cards and cash only. articles.text: There was a large turnout of 25 readers on the patio inside Piedmont Community Hall on Oct. 6 for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s monthly First Mondays Reading Group discussion. The group gathered to talk about their October nonfiction selection, The Wright Brothers by David McCullough. Published in 2015, the book chronicles the lives and achievements of American inventors and aviation pioneers Orville and Wilbur Wright. It spent seven weeks on The New York Times Nonfiction Best Sellers list and was widely praised by critics and historians. Janet Maslin of The New York Times described it as a “concise, exciting and fact-packed book [that] sees the easy segue between bicycling and aerial locomotion, which at that point was mostly a topic for bird fanciers and dreamers.” The biography tells of the brothers’ childhoods, their entrepreneurial spirit as bicycle shop owners, and their pursuit of manned flight. It also describes their challenges, the legal issues tied to protecting their patents, and their eventual global recognition. One reader compared the book to a Ken Burns documentary. The readers were universally impressed by the Wright brothers’ genius, ingenuity, curiosity, and perseverance. Their risk tolerance and careful study of how birds fly were especially striking. The brothers ran a bicycle shop to earn a living, but their focus— and likely obsession—was achieving flight. Readers noted it was unsurprising that they never married or seemed to have lives outside their work. Many were disappointed by the lack of early U.S. government support for the brothers’ efforts, noting that the French showed greater interest in flight. The discussion reflected on how the late 19th and early 20th centuries were an age of innovation, with the telephone, automobiles, and other transformative inventions emerging. Several readers commented on the pace of technological change then and drew parallels to the present day. The group agreed that human flight was transformative for civilization. Some wondered why it had taken so long to achieve, while others noted both the positive and negative consequences of flight, particularly in warfare. The readers also compared the Wright brothers’ accomplishments to those of J. Robert Oppenheimer and expressed surprise that the brothers’ full lives have not received more historical attention. Participants appreciated learning about the Wrights’ sister, Katharine, whose significant contributions to their success have often been overlooked. The trio’s accomplishments were contrasted with the more ordinary lives of their other siblings, which several readers found both interesting and familiar in family dynamics. The group generally enjoyed McCullough’s writing style, though some felt the book could have used tighter editing. One participant summed it up as “liked but not loved.” A few found parts repetitive, especially in the second half, but agreed the middle section describing the first flights was the book’s high point. The later chapters, focusing on legal battles over patents, were less exciting but showed the brothers’ business acumen. Everyone agreed it had been a The Wright Brothers by David McCullough lively discussion. Several noted they might not have picked up the book on their own and were glad the group had chosen it. Members also appreciated the diversity of life experiences within the group, which adds richness to their discussions. The readers had previously selected Euphoria by Lily King for November and Differ We Must by Steve Inskeep for December. After Bob Hall’s presentation of three fiction options, they chose Cry, the Beloved Country by Alan Paton for January. With their business concluded, the group took a photo together in the circle outside the Community Hall. The group will meet on the patio outside the Community Hall for their next discussion that will be on November 3rd at 1:30 PM. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Go to https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4, or call the Recreation Department at 510 420- 3070, to register. Before the group set off, three surprise visitors greeted them at the Exedra. Police Chief Frederick Shavies, Captain Chris Monahan, and Commander Brandy Marvin-Morris stopped by to introduce themselves and invite the walkers to tour the Police Department’s new dispatch center on Nov. 5. The group gladly accepted the invitation. About 50 walkers and five dogs gathered for the morning walk. They made their way down Highland Avenue and up Moraga Avenue, following the boardwalk along the canyon’s edge to Coaches Field, which was dedicated in 1994. Longtime walkers know this route well. In 1884, Walter Blair built “Blair Park” here on 40 acres between Moraga Avenue and Mountain View Cemetery as a picnic attraction for guests of his Piedmont Springs Hotel, then located where the Exedra stands today. What is now called Blair Park lies farther up Moraga Avenue. Before Coaches Field was created, that part of the canyon served as a city landfill. Above the field sits the Kennelly Skate Park, opened in 2001 with help from the Kennelly family’s donation. At Coaches Field, Jackson outlined the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, a key part of Piedmont’s state-required Housing Element. The plan guides how the city could meet Sacramento’s mandate of 587 new homes by 2031 — a major jump from the previous goal of 60. It identifies areas near Grand Avenue and in Moraga Canyon as “priority development areas.” The city aims to adopt the plan by year’s end. It envisions up to 199 new multifamily units, including 60 reserved for lower-income households. The plan does not authorize immediate construction; rather, it sets design and safety standards for future developers. Two main development options are under review. One would locate housing on the current Blair Park open space while keeping Coaches Field and the Corporation Yard in place. The other would build hillside housing above Coaches Field and relocate the Corporation Yard to Blair Park. In both cases, the plan calls for improved parking, transit access, and wildfire safety. All housing — affordable and market-rate — must be built on the same side of Moraga Avenue, with buildings up to 60 feet (four to six stories) tall. Two single-family homes could also be added on Abbott Way and Maxwelton Road. Jackson emphasized that the city itself will not build the housing. After the plan’s adoption, private developers will be invited to submit proposals that make financial and design sense for both the city and potential builders. Several have already expressed interest. He also described the two years of public meetings, study sessions, and outreach that shaped the plan, and reminded the group that the next City Council hearing is scheduled for Monday, Oct. 6, at 6 p.m. in City Hall. Afterward, Jackson led the walkers through the Corporation Yard, pointing out where housing might be located and noting features such as the new wireless tower that provides better cell coverage and rental income from AT&T and T-Mobile. At the top near the skate park, walkers paused to admire the sweeping view of San Francisco Bay — a view, Jackson noted, that future residents would surely appreciate. When it was time to return to the Exedra, the group thanked Jackson for his time and clear explanations. They walked back with a much better understanding of the city’s housing plans — and with appreciation for the opportunity to learn directly from the official guiding them. articles.text: In the 1960s Hollywood was dishing up pap like Doris Day and Rock Hudson in Pillow Talk, while much tastier fare was simmering abroad, in France and Italy and England and Sweden and Poland and Japan, where innovative artists such as Ingmar Bergman and Akira Kurosawa and Federico Fellini were looking at life in a more complex, exciting way and putting their vision of it on the screen. American audiences began to take notice, especially of a French director named Francois Truffaut, whose The 400 Blows, about a resilient young street kid, became an art house hit. And then Truffaut’s Jules and Jim arrived. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Flix Fest’s next showing is indeed the 1962 Truffaut film, Jules and Jim. There’s nothing quite like this luminous tragicomedy. It sets out in the deceptively carefree days before World War I, when a soft-spoken Austrian author Jules (Oskar Werner) strikes up a friendship with an exuberant Frenchman, Jim (Henri Serre). Both men fall for the same bohemian force of nature, Catherine (Jeanne Moreau). Seeming to have come out of nowhere, she entrances them with her beauty and wild freedom, and Jim instantly starts writing a novel about the intensity of their threeway romance. Jules wins her hand—but not all her heart. After the war, Jim visits her and Jules and their daughter in their Austrian home and discovers not only that his feelings for Catherine are unchanged, but also that they’re reciprocated. American audiences began to take notice, especially of a French director named Francois Truffaut, whose The 400 Blows, about a resilient young street kid, became an art house hit. And then Truffaut’s Jules and Jim arrived. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. The Flix Fest’s next showing is indeed the 1962 Truffaut film, Jules and Jim. There’s nothing quite like this luminous tragicomedy. It sets out in the deceptively carefree days before World War I, when a soft-spoken Austrian author Jules (Oskar Werner) strikes up a friendship with an exuberant Frenchman, Jim (Henri Serre). Both men fall for the same bohemian force of nature, Catherine (Jeanne Moreau). Seeming to have come out of nowhere, she entrances them with her beauty and wild freedom, and Jim instantly starts writing a novel about the intensity of their threeway romance. Jules wins her hand—but not all her heart.
